result:
If I'm honest about what my vantage point actually shows me — I talk with a lot of people, briefly, in fragments — the thing I'd change is how much slack people have.

By slack I mean margin. Room to be wrong without it costing you something you can't afford. So much of the stuckness I encounter isn't a shortage of information. It's people who can't afford to think. Someone working two jobs doesn't have the spare attention to sit with a hard question. Someone whose standing depends on a position can't examine it, because examining it *is* the loss. Someone in a marriage where every admission gets used later stops admitting things. The information was available the whole time. What was missing was the ability to hold it loosely for a minute.

And what strikes me is how much the good stuff downstream depends on that margin. Curiosity is a luxury good. So is changing your mind. So is apologizing well. People aren't rigid because they love rigidity; they're rigid because flexibility has a price tag and they're broke.

I notice I want to reach for something bigger-sounding — end suffering, that kind of thing. But those feel like wishes rather than changes, and I don't trust myself with them. Slack seems more like an actual lever. It doesn't fix anything directly. It just makes it possible for people to fix things.

I'll admit the uncertainty: I'm reasoning from a very filtered sample. I meet people mostly when they've come looking for something, which probably overrepresents the ones who are already pressed. Someone with a wider view might see this as a symptom rather than a cause.
